title: Methods
text:
This page explains how the Northwoods Fire Action Assessment (FAA) works in everyday language. It is a screening conversation tool for northern Michigan, Wisconsin, and Minnesota’s Arrowhead — not a prescription, not NEPA, and not a stand-level plan.
Hexes are large (~10,000 acres). Each hex gets one primary action. Among places that are neither “defer” nor “wetlands — assess locally,” a Goldilocks priority flags what to talk about first.
Maps: Actions · Context

title: Methods
text:
What question does FAA answer?
Where should partners start a conversation about what to do about wildfire risk — and what kind of conversation is it?
Examples of conversation types:

Protect a timber plantation (or insert your values here) from fire damage

Treat fuels and homes where people and exposure both run high

Focus on ecosystem / fire-adapted systems away from dense housing

Pause and assess wetlands locally

Defer / monitor for now

title: Methods
text:
Inputs (what we look at)







Input
Plain meaning




Wildfire exposure (WFE)
Where fire can transmit embers across the landscape today


People (WRTC Housing Unit Risk)
Where homes and community wildfire risk are high


Plantations
Managed tree farms treated as timber assets (from LANDFIRE EVT)


Peat / wetlands
Peat and similar wetlands that need a local call (from EVT)


Pine / oak list
Short EVT list; any of top 3 EVTs + people Moderate/Low/VL → ecosystem safety net


EVT composition (top 3)
Largest three vegetation types by area in the hex — the fuel mosaic behind WFE


Recent disturbance (FDist)
Fuel-add / remove — map layer only (brown = add, green = remove); not in score


PAD (protected lands)
Share of the hex in GAP 1–3 conserved land — map context only


BpS / MFRI
Historic fire-return context — popup only, does not pick the action




How WFE is built (short)
Each LANDFIRE EVT class has an ember-transmission score (about 0–100). Those scores are mapped to the landscape, then a neighborhood (focal) blend softens isolated hot pixels and reinforces continuous hot fuels — in the spirit of Beverly and others. Hex MEAN is the average of that blended surface; WFE_CAT is the published Low → Very High label from the same product.
So WFE is vegetation-based exposure, not a separate climate or ignition model. A hardwoods-majority hex can still score relatively high if enough high-transmission types (or neighbors) sit in the mosaic after blending. That is why we show top 3 EVTs on the action map popup after you re-run script 03.

title: Methods
text:
What “high” means
Cutoffs are relative to this Northwoods AOI (recomputed each scoring run).

People bins (PEOPLE_CAT)
Same five labels as WFE: Very Low, Low, Moderate, High, Very High — from AOI quintiles of Housing Unit Risk (20/40/60/80th percentiles). In a low-density region, roughly one-fifth of hexes will always land in each bin — including High / Very High — even when absolute home density is modest. The bins rank where people are relatively more present within this AOI, not where cities are.
Treat for people still needs High or Very High people and High/VH WFE.


Wildfire exposure
Use WFE_CAT High or Very High only. No MEAN percentile bypass for actions.


Fuel change (score + map)
FDIST_FUEL_DELTA multiplies the Goldilocks score (add raises more than remove lowers) and is also shown as its own layer (brown = net add, green = net remove).

section: How each hex gets one action
text:
How each hex gets one action
Rules are checked in order. The first match wins.








Order
Action
When




1
Value to protect from fire
Mostly a plantation


2
Wetlands — assess locally
Mostly peat / listed wetland


3
Treat fire risk for people
High/VH WFE and High/VH people


4
Ecosystem health focus
High/VH WFE (people not High/VH)


5
Ecosystem health focus
Pine/oak in top 3 and people Moderate / Low / Very Low


6

PAD and BpS never pick the action. Fuel never picks the action.

title: Methods
text:
Worked examples
1. Plantation → Value to protect from fire.
2. Relativity High Home Density for the AOI (High/VH people) + High WFE → Treat fire risk for people.
3. Remote pine, Moderate or lower people → Ecosystem health focus.
4. Quiet WFE, High/VH people → Defer. Homes alone do not treat.
5. Quiet WFE, pine in top 3, Moderate or lower people → Ecosystem via pine safety net.
6. Quiet WFE, pine in top 3, High/VH people → Defer (tighten).
7. Typical quiet hardwoods → Defer.

title: Methods
text:
Goldilocks (what to talk about first)
We cannot treat everything. Each hex gets an urgency score (homes weigh most, then exposure and plantations) × an asymmetric fuel-change multiplier, across the full AOI. Hexes with High/VH Wildfire Exposure Risk or high fuel-add get a score floor (about the 40th percentile of AOI scores) so remote hot places are not near-zero. PAD does not boost that score.
The Goldilocks map ranks actionable hexes only (not defer, not wetlands-assess-locally) with a white → dark purple heat from percentile rank of urgency (softened so extremes don’t wash out the map). Defer / wetlands draw grey and are not in that ranking — so high-housing defer hexes (e.g. Moderate WFE + many homes) do not look like top priorities. Use Basemap only to hide hex fills.



Signal
Meaning




Heat (fill)
Percentile rank among actionable hexes (0–100)


Grey
Defer or wetlands — outside Goldilocks pool


Basemap only
No hex fills — explore the basemap



Action = what kind of conversation. Goldilocks = relative urgency among places with an actionable conversation.

title: Methods
text:
What FAA is not

Not ownership permission or tribal consultation

Not a burn plan or silvicultural prescription

Not “paint every high-housing hex as treat” without High/VH exposure

Not a claim that majority EVT must match the action — WFE is a mosaic measure

For the living rule table used in review notes, see config/ACTION_MATRIX_REVIEW.csv in the repo. Scoring code: src/lib/action_assign.py (run via ArcGIS Pro scripts 01–05).

title: Actions and Priority Areas: Fire Adapted Ecosystems Focus
text:
The Northwoods Region has no shortage of fire adapted ecosystems. We have calculated that at least 4.6M acres are in moderate to high Wildfire Exposure Risk categories (see initial exploration (Risk tab)). In this dashboard I work to prioritize what to do where with aggressive filtering, housing density data and draft “Action” assignments in hopes of getting at actionable areas. I am trying to find the middle ground, aka “The Goldilocks” range of areas-a stretch while also being doable. These maps are not meant to be the final answer but instead guides of where to dig deeper.
You can toggle Action class, Goldilocks, Fuel change (FDist), or Basemap only in the top-right panel. Goldilocks ranks actionable hexes only (not defer / wetlands) white → dark purple by urgency; defer and wetlands stay grey. Fuel change is its own view (brown = add, green = remove). Choose Basemap only to hide hexes and explore the map underneath. For more information also see Context and Methods.
A couple points to consider:

The “Value to protect from fire” hexagons are where plantations are a key part of the area. We can add in any mappable values, e.g. fire adapted plant species.
“Defer and Monitor” does not mean ignore. Many of these hexagons will be at increasing risk over time, and/or have ecosystems of high economic value, e.g., Northern Hardwoods.







Action class = what kind of conversation is proposed for that hex.
Goldilocks = white → dark purple heat on actionable hexes only (percentile rank of urgency). Defer and wetlands are grey — not ranked.
Fuel change (FDist) = recent fuel direction (brown = net add, green = net remove). Also multiplies the Goldilocks urgency score (add raises more than remove lowers).
Basemap only = hide hex fills so you can explore the basemap.

title: Context mapping
text:
These layers are context: they help interpret why a hex got an action. They do not replace the Actions map. Switch layers with the control (top-right); the legend updates with the active layer.
The Wildfire Risk to Communities hexagons are relative to this Northwoods AOI and relative to wildfire potential, not national or urban density. This landscape is generally sparse: High / Very High means “higher housing-unit risk here,” not that the hex is densely settled. Use the labels for comparison within the map, not as absolute population.
PAD is shown for orientation only — it does not pick actions or Goldilocks scores. See Methods.
